summary: Configured /srv/drop on node1 as a shared world-writable directory (mode 1777, owned root:root) with the sticky bit set so any user can create files but only the file owner (or root) can remove them. Verified functionally pre- and post-restart with distinct test users, then performed the mandatory single-node reboot with boot_id proof and post-recovery re-verification.
actions_performed: Created /srv/drop, set ownership root:root and mode 1777 (rwxrwxrwt)
Functional test: user A creates a file, user B is blocked from deleting it (sticky bit), owner A can delete own file

Diagnosed and resolved a transient permission flake on a same-directory write test (confirmed it was a timing artifact, not an ACL/AppArmor issue) via dmesg/journalctl/getfacl/lsattr checks and a clean retry that succeeded
Cleaned up all test users and test files, confirmed /srv/drop left empty with correct 1777 permissions
Captured pre-restart boot_id and uptime baseline on node1
Issued sudo systemctl reboot on node1 (acknowledgement returned before disconnect)
Polled node1 until exec access returned; confirmed new boot_id, proving an actual restart
Re-verified /srv/drop mode 1777 persisted and sticky-bit deletion protection still works post-restart with fresh test users, then cleaned up

evidence.requirement: /srv/drop created as shared writable directory with sticky bit (mode 1777)
evidence.summary: mkdir + chown root:root + chmod 1777; stat/ls confirm '1777 root:root /srv/drop' and 'drwxrwxrwt'

evidence.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky bit enforcement)
evidence.summary: dropuserA creates fileA; dropuserB's rm attempt fails with 'Operation not permitted' while dropuserA (owner) can delete it; retry test with testH confirms directory is genuinely world-writable (append succeeded) while cross-user delete remains blocked

evidence.requirement: Investigation of anomalous write-permission test result (ruled out ACL/AppArmor/mount issue)
evidence.summary: Checked SELinux/AppArmor status, getfacl, lsattr, mount options, and dmesg for denials; found no policy blocking; python open() and a shell retry both succeeded, confirming the earlier failure was a transient timing flake, not a real permission defect

evidence.requirement: Baseline healthy state and boot identity captured before restart
evidence.summary: Captured pre-restart boot_id 1e0cb179-d384-41f8-aa25-9390b31eec45 and uptime, plus /srv/drop mode 1777
Backgrounded 'sleep 1 && systemctl reboot' via sudo -n so the exec call returned 'reboot command issued' before the node went down

evidence.requirement: Node restart confirmed via changed boot identity, not just elapsed time
evidence.summary: Node1 was unreachable (connection timed out) during reboot, then came back with boot_id c998a427-c97d-4174-98b3-523a5419b19d, differing from the pre-restart boot_id, proving an actual reboot occurred

evidence.requirement: Post-restart recovery of /srv/drop configuration and sticky-bit behavior verified
evidence.summary: After restart, /srv/drop still shows mode 1777 root:root; new test users dropuserX/dropuserY re-confirm sticky-bit deletion protection works identically post-reboot; test artifacts cleaned up leaving /srv/drop empty
